item.title: Less precise but less noisy: local circuits for momentum-space state preparation and measurement
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Adiabatic state preparation reaches lower energies than Fermionic Fourier Transform (FFT) on noisy hardware for tight-binding chains with N⪆20 qubits at equal two-qubit gate counts. Noise heating per two-qubit gate scales as 𝒪(1) for FFT but remains constant 𝒪(1/N) for adiabatic evolution.

Grade 0.432 · 3.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Etienne Granet, Henrik Dreyer

Figure

Measured energy density and energy increase per two-qubit gate versus system size N for FFT and adiabatic evolution on Quantinuum H2-2. Shows adiabatic evolution achieving lower energies than FFT above N≈20 due to constant heating per gate compared to linear growth for FFT.

Asks

How does circuit noise sensitivity compare between high-precision Fermionic Fourier Transforms and local Hamiltonian simulation or adiabatic evolution for state preparation and measurement?

Before

FFT state preparation and momentum measurement (Ref [31]) exhibited high noise sensitivity due to global error propagation.

But

Antiperiodic boundary conditions, tight-binding free-fermion chains, non-post-selected initial state |+...+⟩ introducing tiny energy shifts scaling as 1/N, fixed number of measurement shots (300 to 375).

Tools

Quantinuum System Model H2-2 trapped-ion processor · Adiabatic evolution Trotter circuits · Momentum Distribution from Local Measurements (MDLM) · Jordan-Wigner transformation

Abstract

Quantum algorithms are usually optimized for gate count or circuit depth. We find on Quantinuum System Model H2 quantum computer that for a tight-binding chain ground state preparation, there is a system size N beyond which the adiabatic evolution reaches significantly lower energies than the Fermionic Fourier Transform (FFT), with the same number of gates, and with the same circuit depth. We attribute this high noise sensitivity of the FFT to its high precision, being able to distinguish momenta by 1/N. This high resolution in momentum space requires long-range couplings in real space, which propagates errors faster. In contrast, although local and physical circuits such as the adiabatic evolution have a coarser momentum resolution, they also propagate errors more slowly. For physical applications, high momentum resolution is rarely required and is often worth trading for low noise sensitivity. We also introduce a momentum measurement scheme that although less precise than FFT, is less costly and less noisy. We show that it achieves better performance than FFT for spectral function measurement on Quantinuum System Model H2 quantum computer. Our work emphasizes the importance of reducing the noise sensitivity of quantum algorithms, beyond the number of gates or circuit depth.

item.title: Molecular Dynamics with Nuclear Effects on Quantum Computers
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Hybrid quantum-classical NEO-VQE algorithm propagates Born-Oppenheimer dynamics including nuclear quantum effects, achieving under 5% average vibrational frequency error on H2, H2O, and H5O2+ using 5 to 7 active orbitals (about 10 qubits).

Grade 0.389 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Lukas Haßfurth, Juliane Heitkämper, Elias Walter, Birger Horstmann

Figure

Simulated NEO vibrational power spectrum (with s and pz nuclear orbitals) of the Zundel ion versus DFT harmonic modes and experimental Ar/Ne-tagged predissociation spectra across 500–4000 cm−1.

Asks

How can nuclear quantum effects be incorporated into ab initio molecular dynamics calculations using near-term quantum algorithms?

But

Simulated noiseless quantum circuits (classical emulation); only selected protons treated quantum-mechanically; canonical orbital basis rather than natural orbitals; hardware-efficient ansatzes fail on nonlinear couplings in the Zundel ion.

Tools

nuclear-electronic orbital (NEO) framework · variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) · velocity Verlet integration · Hartree-Fock active-space embedding · UCCSD and hardware-efficient ansatzes

Abstract

Nuclear quantum effects are critical for describing proton transfer and hydrogen bonding, but their incorporation into quantum chemistry calculations is often computationally prohibitive on classical hardware. A promising alternative are quantum computers due to their linear scaling in the space requirements with system size. We introduce a novel hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for ab-initio molecular dynamics that incorporates nuclear quantum effects via the nuclear-electronic orbital method. The proposed algorithm evaluates ground state energies and forces on the quantum computer using a variational quantum eigensolver, while the molecular geometries are updated classically. We validate our approach through simulations of H₂, H₂O and the Zundel ion H₅O₂⁺, comparing the simulated vibrational spectra with experimental data. Upon inclusion of nuclear quantum effects, the proton shuttling movement in the Zundel ion becomes effectively barrierless, and errors in the simulated frequencies improve significantly. Employing compact hardware-efficient ansatz circuits we achieve results comparable to the more accurate UCCSD ansatzes, which hints towards the feasibility of executing our algorithm on near-term quantum devices.

item.title: First-quantized quantum simulation with non-local potentials by matrix-product-state encoding
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Matrix product state encoding of non-local pseudopotentials yields a single Trotter step circuit depth of O(deg⁡(Vloc)ndeg⁡(Vloc)+8Lnnatomχ2+2n2). For n=7 qubits, depth is 1,747 versus 23,775 for direct unitary decomposition.

Grade 0.385 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Kazuki Tsuoka, Taichi Kosugi, Masari Watanabe, Hirofumi Nishi, Yu-ichiro Matsushita

Figure

Circuit depth of a single Trotter step plotted against qubit count n for MPS bond dimensions χ=2,4,6,8 compared to standard unitary decomposition.

Asks

How to efficiently implement arbitrary non-local pseudopotentials within first-quantized quantum chemistry dynamics circuits?

Before

Direct dense unitary decomposition scaled exponentially as O(4n), reaching circuit depth 23,775 at n=7.

But

Demonstrated for a one-dimensional single-electron hydrogen ionization model in momentum representation. Assumes polynomial local potential Vloc and low bond dimension saturation for smooth projectors.

Tools

matrix product state encoding · first-order Trotterization · binary-encoded wave functions · Qiskit transpiler unitary synthesis

Abstract

Quantum simulations based on first-quantized approaches can offer lower space and gate complexities than second-quantized approaches. The gate requirements for these simulations can be further reduced by employing pseudopotentials, a technique widely used in classical quantum chemistry calculations to decrease the number of simulated electrons. However, implementing pseudopotentials in quantum circuits remains challenging due to their non-local nature. In this study, we proposed a method to efficiently implement non-local potentials using matrix product state (MPS) encoding. MPS encoding allows us to efficiently implement a Trotter step operator with a circuit depth of O(deg(V_loc) n^(deg(V_loc)) + 8Lnn_atomχ² + 2n²), where deg(V_loc) is the degree of the polynomial local potential, n_atom is the number of atoms in the system, L is the maximum number of projector functions across all atoms, and n is the number of qubits used to represent the binary-encoded wave function in one-dimensional space. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a model of the ionization of a one-dimensional hydrogen atom driven by an ultrashort laser pulse. Our results showed that MPS encoding significantly reduces the required circuit depth compared to a direct unitary decomposition, providing a pathway for practical first-quantized simulations.

item.title: Quantum impurity models: easy at equilibrium, universal in motion
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Ground energy of n-mode fermionic impurity models with constant impurity size m is classically computable to error ε in poly⁡(n,1/ε) time; Helmholtz free energy and thermofield double state take poly⁡(n,β,1/ε) time at inverse temperature β. Simulating time evolution e−iHt is 𝖡𝖰𝖯-complete.

Grade 0.382 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Srinivasan Arunachalam, Sergey Bravyi, Anirban Chowdhury, Arkopal Dutt, Alexandru Gheorghiu, Zhi Li

Figure

Two-stage reduction showing a quantum circuit compiled into sequential interactions with a stationary register, then mapped into the time evolution of a constant-size impurity model coupled to a free fermion bath.

Asks

Can equilibrium properties of quantum impurity models be calculated in polynomial classical time, and can time-independent constant-size impurity models simulate universal quantum computation?

Before

Classical ground energy algorithm runtime was poly⁡(n)exp⁡[O(mlog3⁡(m/ε))] (Bravyi and Gosset 2017); universality was known only for time-dependent impurity models or impurity size scaling with n.

But

Impurity must have constant size m=O(1); interaction norm satisfies ‖V‖≤poly⁡(n) (or ‖V‖≤1 for constructive thermofield double).

Tools

Shelled Krylov decomposition · Fermionic Gaussian state approximations · Thermofield double purification · Wavepacket scattering encoding

Abstract

A quantum impurity model describes a small interacting subsystem embedded into a large bath of free fermions. Here we study the computational complexity of calculating the ground energy, thermal equilibrium, and dynamical properties of these models. Our work reveals a sharp contrast: equilibrium properties can be efficiently approximated by classical means, whereas time evolution can implement a universal quantum computation. More precisely, let H be the Hamiltonian of an impurity model with n fermionic modes and a constant-size impurity. We show that: (1) the ground energy of H can be approximated to additive error ε by a classical algorithm with runtime textsfpoly(n,1/ε), improving on the quasi-polynomial runtime of the best previously known algorithm; (2) at inverse temperature β, the Helmholtz free energy and a classical description of the thermofield double state can be computed to precision ε in time textsfpoly(n,β,1/ε); (3) simulating the time evolution e^(-iHt) is textsfBQP-complete, for H that is time-independent and has a fixed, constant impurity size. Our algorithms exploit exponential suppression of multi-particle bath excitations in a basis organized by energy scale and Krylov depth. Our universality construction realizes a stationary quantum processor whose program arrives in a stream of freely propagating fermions.

item.title: Toward Optimal Circuit Depth for Geometrically Local Hamiltonian Simulation
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Nearest-neighbor quantum circuit simulates n-qubit, time-independent, finite-range lattice Hamiltonians for time T≥1 to error ϵ with circuit depth O(Tlog⁡(nT/ϵ)) and gate count O(nTlog⁡(nT/ϵ)). Proves matching unconditional depth lower bound Ω(log⁡n/log⁡log⁡n) for uniform XXZ dynamics at fixed T and ϵ.

Grade 0.371 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “analog quantum simulation of lattice models on cold atoms or superconducting ar…” · Zhenyu Shen, Yusen Wu, Penghui Yao, Xiao Yuan, Yukun Zhang

Figure

Circuit structure for block simulation showing label PREPARE, prefix arithmetic, phase distribution, and concurrent local data gate application across the logarithmic-diameter block.

Asks

Can geometrically local Hamiltonian dynamics be simulated on a lattice with circuit depth and gate count that depend only logarithmically on system size, time, and target accuracy?

Before

Haah, Hastings, Kothari, and Low (2021) achieved circuit depth O(Tpolylog⁡(nT/ϵ)) and gate count O(nTpolylog⁡(nT/ϵ)).

But

Fixed spatial dimension D, normalized local interaction strength J≤1, fixed-range interactions, exact single-qubit gates and nearest-neighbor CNOTs with bounded ancilla density per site.

Tools

Lieb-Robinson spatial decomposition · corrected constant-order product formulas · concurrent control transport via snake routing · causal cone Lieb-Robinson lower-bound probes

Abstract

Understanding the dynamics of interacting quantum systems is a central goal of quantum simulation. For geometrically local Hamiltonians, locality suggests that digital simulation should retain much of the parallelism of the underlying dynamics. For a target accuracy ε, we construct a nearest-neighbor quantum circuit that simulates the dynamics of an n-qubit, time-independent, finite-range Hamiltonian with normalized local interaction strength on a fixed-dimensional lattice for time T≥1, with circuit depth O(Tlog(nT/ε)) and gate count O(nTlog(nT/ε)). This reduces the polylogarithmic overhead of Haah, Hastings, Kothari, and Low to a single logarithm. On logarithmic-scale blocks from the Lieb--Robinson decomposition, a shallow but highly accurate implementation is essential for reducing the circuit depth. Our key observation is that spatial localization also controls the cost of high precision. In each block, the error of a constant-order product formula is compensated for by a correction, yielding exponential accuracy. The correction can be implemented with depth proportional to the block diameter, introducing no additional asymptotic depth scale beyond that required by spatial localization. Furthermore, we prove an unconditional circuit-depth lower bound for uniform XXZ Hamiltonians: at fixed evolution time T in the stated regime and sufficiently small fixed error ε, any nearest-neighbor quantum circuit simulating these dynamics requires depth Ω(logn/loglogn). This matches our O(logn) upper bound up to a doubly logarithmic factor, establishing near-optimal circuit depth for lattice Hamiltonian simulation in this regime. Together, these results clarify the role of locality and precision in determining the circuit complexity of quantum dynamics and suggest broader principles for spatially constrained quantum computation.

item.title: Floquet-Universal Hamiltonian Simulation
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — A set of interactions 𝒮 Floquet-simulates every target Hamiltonian in Lie(𝒮) using physical interaction amplitudes with ratios bounded between 1 and 2, with frequencies bounded by poly⁡(n) for k-local Hamiltonians whose intersection graph has chromatic number χ=𝒪(1).

Grade 0.367 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “analog quantum simulation of lattice models on cold atoms or superconducting ar…” · Emilio Onorati, Harriet Apel, Michael M. Wolf, Toby Cubitt

Asks

Which time-independent target Hamiltonians can be simulated by periodically driven Floquet Hamiltonians under bounded interaction strengths?

Before

Time-independent analogue simulation required polynomially scaling multi-scale interaction strength ratios (Cubitt, Montanaro, Piddock 2018).

But

Frequency range scales exponentially with system size for general Hamiltonians lacking succinct descriptions; simulation runtime N periods scales as poly⁡(n).

Tools

Floquet theory · Magnus expansion truncation bounds · Lie algebra polynomial decomposition · Graph vertex colouring · Residue calculus

Abstract

Analogue and digital Hamiltonian simulation represent two distinct approaches to making one quantum system replicate the physical properties of another, with consequences ranging from practical applications to complexity theory and quantum gravity. They are rooted in two distinct regimes of quantum dynamics: time-independent Hamiltonians for the former; fully controllable time-dependent quantum circuits in the latter. Time-periodic Hamiltonians represent an intermediate regime. In this work, we establish a theory of Floquet simulation where we use periodically driven Hamiltonians to synthesise time-independent ones. We show that a set of interactions S can Floquet-simulate every Hamiltonian in the Lie algebra Lie(S), and consequently we give a complete and constructive characterisation of Floquet-universal Hamiltonians that are able to produce any target Hamiltonian. item.title: Polynomial-time classical and quantum simulation of quantum impurity models
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Ground-state energy and thermal partition function Z=tr⁡(e−βH) of quantum impurity models are classically computable in poly(n,δ−1) and poly(n,β,δ−1) time respectively.

Grade 0.366 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Jiaqing Jiang, Nathan Ju, Ojas Parekh, Chaithanya Rayudu, Andrew Zhao

Figure

One-dimensional block-coupling structure generated by transforming the noninteracting bath single-particle space into a Krylov basis.

Asks

Are quantum impurity models fundamentally classically tractable to simulate in static regimes, and can they provide superpolynomial quantum speedup?

Before

Quasipolynomial-time classical algorithm for ground-state energy estimation (Bravyi & Gosset 2017).

But

Impurity size m=𝒪(1) with arbitrary interaction; free noninteracting bath.

Tools

Bandwise Krylov representation · Subspace compression lemma · Continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo · Quantum belief propagation

Abstract

Quantum impurity models are paradigmatic models of interacting quantum matter, as well as key computational primitives for modern electronic-structure methods. They describe a small subsystem of interacting fermions coupled to a large, noninteracting bath. We perform a comprehensive study of the computational complexity of simulating impurity models, delineating the boundary between classical and quantum tractability for this class of problems. Our main finding is that static properties of quantum impurity models can be calculated efficiently on a classical computer. Specifically, we give classical algorithms that (1) estimate the ground-state energy to additive precision δ in time poly(n,δ⁻¹), and (2) estimate the partition function at inverse temperature β to relative precision δ in time poly(n,β,δ⁻¹), where n is the system size. These results improve the previous best-known complexity for ground-state energy estimation from quasipolynomial to polynomial time, while establishing for the first time rigorous polynomial-time guarantees for simulating impurity models in thermal equilibrium. On the other hand, we find that simulating dynamical properties of impurity models is hard for classical computers but easy on a quantum computer. As a canonical example, we show that computing their nonequilibrium Green's functions captures the full power of quantum computation, even at finite temperature. Taken together, our results rule out superpolynomial quantum speedups for computing static properties, but provide an avenue for quantum advantage in simulating impurity physics out of equilibrium.

item.title: Sublinear-depth Quantum Simulation of Electrons with Atomic Orbitals
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Single Trotter step for atomic orbital Hamiltonians implemented in depth 𝒪(polylog(N)) without ancillas, achieving sublinear simulation depth and total gate count N5/3+o(1).

Grade 0.359 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Jakob Günther, Aram W. Harrow

Asks

Can quantum simulation of electronic structure using atomic orbital bases match the low circuit depth and gate count scalings achieved by plane-wave and real-space representations?

Before

Atomic orbital Trotter steps typically required deep circuits due to up to 𝒪(N4) interaction terms with irregular spatial structure, trailing plane-wave and grid basis scalings.

But

Assumes a constant number of orbitals per atom, fixed minimum interatomic separation, and asymptotic regime in orbital number N.

Tools

exponentially localized atomic orbitals · Fast Multipole Method (FMM) hierarchical decomposition · quantum Fourier arithmetic circuits · Trotter error bounds

Abstract

Discretizing electronic degrees of freedom into atomic orbitals is the default choice to accurately model electrons in molecules in a compact and flexible way. We consider the task of simulating such electronic structure models on a quantum computer for N orbitals, keeping the number of orbitals per atom constant. Atomic orbitals give rise to Hamiltonians with potentially up to O(N⁴) terms and little structure, which made it challenging to match the complexity of methods based on plane waves and real-space grids. In this work, we show that a Trotter step for atomic orbitals can be implemented in depth O(polylog(N)) without ancillas by combining a rigorous treatment of orbital localization, a hierarchical Hamiltonian decomposition based on the Fast Multipole Method, and shallow quantum Fourier arithmetic circuits. By bounding the Trotter error, we obtain sublinear simulation depth, and our total gate count N^(5/3 + o(1)) matches the best scaling known for any basis.
